Adult Spangled cichlids collected from the southern basin of Lake Tanganyika attain a maximum total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a size that aligns closely with the upper range reported for other members of the genus Limnochromis. This ultimate body dimension is reached only after several years of growth in the stable, warm waters of the lake’s littoral zone. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically cease somatic expansion once this plateau is attained, with subsequent energy being channeled primarily into reproductive activities. The species exhibits a moderately elongated body form, and the 13 centimeter [Li = 13 centimeter] maximum length serves as a reliable diagnostic character for distinguishing mature adults from juvenile conspecifics during underwater visual censuses. Growth rates in this cichlid are comparatively slow relative to some haplochromine species, reflecting the energetically conservative life-history strategy common among deep-water lamprologine and limnochromine lineages inhabiting the oligotrophic pelagic zone of Lake Tanganyika.

Sexual maturation in the Spangled cichlid is marked by the attainment of a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], at which point individuals begin undergoing gonadal recrudescence and become capable of participating in the breeding population. This length-at-puberty threshold (7 centimeters) [Lp = 7 centimeters] was determined from histological examination of preserved specimens collected across multiple wet and dry seasons, revealing the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males at this size. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty averages 4.9 grams [Wwp = 4.9 grams], a body mass that reflects the modest energy reserves required to initiate reproductive investment in this relatively small-bodied cichlid. The transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one incorporating gamete production occurs when individuals have accumulated sufficient lipid stores, typically during their second year of life under the thermal conditions prevailing in Lake Tanganyika.

Embryonic development commences within a small, demersal egg, and the resulting yolk-sac larva emerges at a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 0.023 grams [Wwb = 0.023 grams], a value estimated from the dimensions of fertilized ova. This neonatal mass (0.023 grams) [Wwb = 0.023 grams] is comparable to those observed in other substrate-spawning Tanganyikan cichlids that produce clutches of moderate fecundity, reflecting a trade-off between offspring size and number. The larvae remain dependent on their yolk reserves for several days post-hatching before transitioning to exogenous feeding on microzooplankton. Brood care in this species is extensive, with both parents guarding the free-swimming larvae and later the small juveniles, a behavioral investment that may compensate for the initially diminutive size of the newly hatched individuals. The energetic cost of producing such small neonates is offset by the potential for larger clutch sizes, an adaptive strategy in the variable food environment of Lake Tanganyika.

Reproductive output in the Spangled cichlid has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], which closely approximate the mean annual temperature of their natural habitat. Gravid females produce clutches of moderate size, and the observed spawning frequency reaches approximately 0.75 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.75 clutches per year]. Each clutch contains around 4 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains around 4 eggs], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.82 offspring per day when the two factors are combined. This reproductive strategy is relatively modest compared to many r-selected cichlids, consistent with the species’ K-selected life-history approach that emphasizes parental care and offspring survival over sheer numerical output. The spawning interval is tightly linked to the 27 °C [T = 27 °C] thermal regime; deviations of even a few degrees can extend the inter-brood period markedly. Observations from long-term aquarium studies confirm that females require a recovery phase between spawnings to replenish somatic condition, limiting the annual reproductive effort.

Longevity records from both field-marked populations and captive maintenance programs reveal a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] for the Spangled cichlid when held at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This lifespan (approximately 6 years) [am = approximately 6 years] is intermediate among Tanganyikan cichlids, placing the species between short-lived annual killifish and the long-lived predatory lates perches at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Senescence in older individuals is characterized by a gradual decline in reproductive output and a loss of body condition, particularly in females that have undergone multiple spawning seasons. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown, senescent adult is approximately 30.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.8 grams], representing the maximum somatic investment possible under the species’ energetic constraints. This asymptotic body mass (approximately 30.8 grams) [Wwi = approximately 30.8 grams] is achieved only after several years of growth, and few individuals in the wild reach this upper limit due to predation pressure and the energetic demands of repeated reproduction.
